title: People, not particles: behaviour and choice
summary: People choose routes, walk in groups, follow familiar paths and respond to information. Crowd behaviour is social, and 'panic' is rare. Good management works with that behaviour.
outcomes: explain why people often use familiar routes even when others are free
describe how groups and social identity shape crowd behaviour
explain why information, not just space, changes how crowds move
challenge the myth of mass panic with evidence
narration_en: Physics explains a lot about crowds, but people are not particles. They have goals, habits and friends. When people leave a building, many head for the door they came in by, even when another exit is closer and empty. Families and friends walk together, and a group moves at the pace of its slowest member. People look at what others do and follow them. In emergencies, research shows that people mostly stay calm and help each other, partly because they come to feel part of a shared group. Real problems come from missing or confusing information, delays in deciding to move, and designs that send everyone the same way. That is why good crowd management is not only about widths and capacities. It is about signs that people understand, announcements they trust, stewards they can ask, and routes that match what people naturally do. In this module you will explore how behaviour changes evacuation times, and why the myth of mass panic is so persistent and so misleading.
narration_ar: تفسّر الفيزياء كثيراً عن الحشود، لكن الناس ليسوا جسيمات. لديهم أهداف وعادات وأصدقاء. فعندما يغادر الناس مبنى، يتجه كثير منهم إلى الباب الذي دخلوا منه، حتى لو كان مخرج آخر أقرب وفارغاً. وتسير العائلات والأصدقاء معاً، وتتحرك المجموعة بسرعة أبطأ أفرادها. وينظر الناس إلى ما يفعله الآخرون فيتبعونهم. وفي حالات الطوارئ، تُظهر الأبحاث أن الناس يبقون في الغالب هادئين ويساعد بعضهم بعضاً، ويعود ذلك جزئياً إلى شعورهم بالانتماء إلى مجموعة مشتركة. أما المشكلات الحقيقية فتأتي من المعلومات الناقصة أو المربكة، والتأخر في قرار التحرك، والتصاميم التي ترسل الجميع في الاتجاه نفسه. لهذا فإن الإدارة الجيدة للحشود لا تقتصر على العروض والسعات. بل تشمل لافتات يفهمها الناس، وإعلانات يثقون بها، ومنظّمين يمكن سؤالهم، وطرقاً تتوافق مع ما يفعله الناس بطبيعتهم. ستستكشف في هذه الوحدة كيف يغيّر السلوك أزمنة الإخلاء، ولماذا تستمر أسطورة الذعر الجماعي وكم هي مضللة.

diagram.title: What shapes how people move
diagram.caption: Goals, habits, groups and information shape choices; those choices shape the flow.

nodes.label: Goals
nodes.detail: Destination, urgency and desired speed differ: commuters hurry, families stroll, pilgrims follow a ritual sequence.

nodes.label: Habits and familiarity
nodes.detail: People prefer routes and exits they know, often the one they arrived by (affiliation; Sime 1985).

nodes.label: Groups
nodes.detail: Most people at events are in groups. Groups walk at the pace of the slowest member and do not split easily.

nodes.label: Information
nodes.detail: Clear, early, trusted information shortens decision times and spreads people across routes.

nodes.label: Choices
nodes.detail: Decisions about which way, which exit and when to move. Their sum is the crowd's distribution across routes.

nodes.label: Shared identity
nodes.detail: In emergencies people often develop a shared identity and help each other (Drury, Cocking and Reicher 2009).

nodes.label: Crowd outcome
nodes.detail: Uneven use of exits, long pre-movement times and counterflows lengthen evacuations and create hot spots.

tour.text: People bring goals, habits and companions with them.
These shape their choices: which route, which exit, when to move.
Information steers those choices, if it is clear, early and trusted.
In emergencies, shared identity usually makes people cooperate rather than panic.
Add the choices up and you get the crowd's outcome: queues, times and risk.

sections.heading: Familiar routes
sections.html:
Studies of evacuations and exit choice show that many people head for the exit they know, often the one they entered by, even if another is nearer and free. Sime (1985) called this affiliation with familiar places and people. The result: one exit queues while another stands empty.

evacuation time ≈ time of the slowest exit to empty

sections.heading: Groups
sections.html: At events, most people come with family or friends. Groups move together, walk more slowly, and form walking shapes such as a line abreast or a V (Moussaïd et al. 2010). In evacuations, people look for their group before leaving, which adds to pre-movement time.

sections.heading: The myth of panic
sections.html: Films and headlines show crowds 'panicking'. Research on real emergencies finds the opposite: people are mostly orderly and helpful, and selfish behaviour is rare (Drury, Cocking and Reicher 2009). What looks like panic in a crush is people being pushed by forces they cannot resist. Blaming panic draws attention away from design, information and management.

sections.heading: Information changes movement
sections.html: People decide using what they see and hear. Clear signs in the crowd's languages, announcements from trusted voices, and visible stewards shorten decision times and balance routes. Poor information, or none, is a cause in many incidents: crowds keep pushing forward because those at the back cannot see what is happening at the front.

callouts.title: Explore it
callouts.html: Use the explorer: with 80% of people heading for the main entrance, how much longer does the evacuation take than with an even split?

callouts.title: Pilgrims and information
callouts.html: At the Hajj, pilgrims come from over 150 countries and speak many languages. Group leaders, colour-coded signs and staggered schedules are part of how information reaches them.

explorer.intro: 1,200 people leave through two equal exits. Change the share heading for the entrance they came in by.
explorer.predict: If 90% use the main entrance, roughly how much longer does it take than an even split: 10%, 50% or 80%?

code.title: Familiar exit bias
code.source:
N, cap = 1200, 3.0          # people, and people per second per exit
for share in [0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9]:
    a, b = N * share, N * (1 - share)
    t = max(a / cap + 20, b / cap + 25)   # walking time 20 s and 25 s
    print(f'{share:.0%} at the main entrance: everyone out in {t/60:.1f} min')
code.explain: Total time is set by the slower exit. Try changing the walking times.
code.expected:
50% at the main entrance: everyone out in 3.8 min
...
90% at the main entrance: everyone out in 6.3 min

takeaways: People often choose familiar routes, which leaves some exits underused.
Groups move together and slow evacuations.
Mass panic is a myth; cooperation is the norm, and crushes are physical.
Clear, early, trusted information changes how crowds move.
